title: Hard to be called a Muslim
word: Hard to be called a Muslim
hook: it is hard to be called a true Muslim; first love the faith and let go of pride (Majh ki Var, ang 141)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dark age is a knife, and your line was a knife of an age. Where did you use a little power honestly? Today the ballad turns from kings to the name a person carries. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

A cast-iron pan comes out of the back of a cupboard, orange with rust. Steel wool, hot water, a lot of patience, and slowly the dark metal shows again. Nobody calls it clean until it is. Guru Nanak lived among Hindus and Muslims, and in his ballad in Majh he speaks to his Muslim neighbors in the words of their own faith. He doesn't tell anyone to stop being a Muslim. He says something harder, given here in plain English, not word for word: it's difficult to be called a Muslim. Only if you truly are one should you be called one. Today: hard to be called a Muslim, and what Guru Nanak says it takes.
screen: `A RUSTY PAN, SCOURED.` → `NANAK SPEAKS TO HIS NEIGHBORS.` → `HARD TO BE CALLED A MUSLIM.`

segments.voice: Here's how the salok goes on, again in plain English. First, let the faith be sweet to you. Scrape away pride in your wealth, the way rust is scraped from metal. Become a true follower of the faith, and be rid of doubt about death and life. Accept God's will as above your head. Trust the Creator, and lose your self-importance. Be kind to every living being, says Nanak, and then you may be called a Muslim. Notice how high the bar is, and notice whose bar it is. Listen to the words it chooses: din, faith; raza, God's will; mihar, mercy. These are words his Muslim neighbors used for their own faith. Guru Nanak isn't inventing a new standard and laying it over his neighbors. He's taking their own words seriously, and asking that they be lived all the way through. A few lines before, on ang one hundred forty, he does the same with the outward signs. In paraphrase: let mercy be your mosque, faith your prayer mat, and honest living your Quran. Modesty, good conduct, truth: each one a practice of the faith, lived inside. Second, notice who the salok is not aimed against. It isn't mocking anyone. Elsewhere on this path you've heard Nanak ask the same of pandits and yogis: live what your name promises. Muslims, here, are honored by being held to their own best words. Third, notice the order. First, sweetness. Before rules, before outward signs, the faith has to taste sweet. The salok calls this hard. It doesn't call it impossible. That's today's line: hard to be true.
screen: `FIRST, LET THE FAITH BE SWEET.` · `SCRAPE AWAY PRIDE LIKE RUST.` · `MERCY BE YOUR MOSQUE.` · `BE KIND TO EVERY BEING.` · then, large: `HARD TO BE TRUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live your own faith more truly. Sit, and let your breath slow. Name, quietly, what you're called: the faith you belong to, or the one you're learning, or a simpler name if you have none, like friend, parent, neighbor. Then ask, gently: what does that name promise? Find one word in it. Kindness, honesty, patience, mercy. Hold that word for a few breaths. Then picture one small way to live it today, not someday. If you pray, you can offer that word to God in the way your own tradition prays. The bell holds the time.
Hard to be called a Muslim. Guru Nanak's salok in Majh ki Var: let the faith be sweet, scrape away pride, accept God's will, be kind to every being, and then be called by the name. Today's word.
screen: `HARD TO BE CALLED A MUSLIM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: hard to be true. Today, choose one promise your own name makes, whatever that name is, and keep it once, on purpose, where it costs you something. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: These saloks are sung and read as part of Majh ki Var in the Guru Granth Sahib, and in katha they are explained as Guru Nanak asking people of every faith to live what their own faith teaches.

match.prompt: what's inside the salok — tap the pairs.

myth: Guru Nanak tells Muslims to stop being Muslims
he asks them to be Muslims truly, in their own faith's words: sweetness, surrender, mercy.
the salok says kindness to every living being is part of the name
be kind to every being, says Nanak, and then be called a Muslim.
the salok calls living up to the name impossible
it calls it hard, and then lays out the steps.

fork.setup: you carry the name of your faith. in Guru Nanak's salok, what comes first?
options: letting the faith be sweet to you.
fork.reveal: first, let the faith be sweet; then scrape away pride, accept God's will, and be kind to every being.

original.note: musalman kahavan muskal: 'it is hard to be called a Muslim', the salok's opening.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line criticizing another faith.
what it means: Guru Nanak holds Muslims to Islam's own best words, and the same bar runs through his words to every path.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear sound-play in the salok, musalman, muskal (hard), maskal (a polisher's tool for rust), so the name itself carries the work.

notes: Ang 141 salok paraphrased from ਮੁਸਲਮਾਣੁ ਕਹਾਵਣੁ ਮੁਸਕਲੁ ਜਾ ਹੋਇ ਤਾ ਮੁਸਲਮਾਣੁ ਕਹਾਵੈ ॥ ਅਵਲਿ ਅਉਲਿ ਦੀਨੁ ਕਰਿ ਮਿਠਾ ਮਸਕਲ ਮਾਨਾ ਮਾਲੁ ਮੁਸਾਵੈ ... ਤਉ ਨਾਨਕ ਸਰਬ ਜੀਆ ਮਿਹਰੰਮਤਿ ਹੋਇ ਤ ਮੁਸਲਮਾਣੁ ਕਹਾਵੈ. 'Scrape away pride like rust' reads ਮਸਕਲ as a polishing tool; please confirm this reading and the trapdoor's sound-play claim, or cut.
Ang 140 salok (ਮਿਹਰ ਮਸੀਤਿ ਸਿਦਕੁ ਮੁਸਲਾ ਹਕੁ ਹਲਾਲੁ ਕੁਰਾਣੁ) is paraphrased; please confirm the Ang (140 vs 141).

Sensitive day: written so the salok honors Muslims by their own faith's words and never ranks Islam or suggests switching. A Keeper and, ideally, a reader from the Islam path should check the framing.
'Guru Nanak lived among Hindus and Muslims' is general; 'Elsewhere on this path you've heard Nanak ask the same of pandits and yogis' refers to the Oankar and Sidh Gosht days.
Original: please confirm Gurmukhi and the pronunciation guide.

Editor pass: new hook (a rusty pan scoured) so the name-badge image does not run into day 1172's name-sticker hook; 'every step uses a word that belongs to Islam itself' (which counted the Punjabi 'Creator') replaced with the salok's own words din, raza, mihar; 'fear of death' changed to 'doubt' (bharam); match pairs moved off the Ang 140 mosque line already taught in years 1 and 2; trapdoor sound-play hedged; howItsDone 'often' cut.
